what_its_for: This medicine is used to treat certain types of breast cancer and stomach cancer that test positive for a protein called HER2. HER2-positive cancers grow faster because they have too much of this protein. This medicine works by attaching to HER2 and helping your immune system find and destroy cancer cells. It is often used alone or with other cancer medicines.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as a shot (injection) under the skin, usually in your thigh or belly area. A nurse or doctor will give you this injection in a clinic or hospital setting. You will NOT inject this yourself at home. Each injection typically takes about 5 to 8 minutes. You may be watched for at least 30 minutes after your first injection to make sure you do not have a bad reaction. Do not try to give this medicine to yourself.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your body weight, the type of cancer you have, and how well you respond to treatment. The most common schedule is once every 3 weeks (every 21 days). Your first dose may be higher (called a loading dose), and follow-up doses may be slightly lower (called maintenance doses). Always follow your doctor's instructions exactly and never skip a scheduled appointment without calling your care team first.
missed_dose: If you miss or skip an appointment for your injection, call your doctor or cancer care team right away to reschedule as soon as possible. Do not wait until your next scheduled dose. Your doctor may adjust your dosing schedule depending on how long you have waited. It is very important to stay on schedule to keep the medicine working properly.
storage: This medicine is stored and handled by your healthcare team. It must be kept in a refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C). It should NOT be frozen or shaken. The vials must be kept away from direct light. You do not need to store this medicine at home. If for any reason you have a vial at home, keep it refrigerated and bring it to your clinic if you are unsure how to handle it.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor about ALL medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, as some drugs may interact with this medicine. Avoid becoming pregnant while using this medicine and for 7 months after your last dose, as it can seriously harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine and for 7 months after your last dose. Avoid receiving live vaccines during treatment without talking to your doctor first.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: shortness of breath, chest pain, or a fast or irregular heartbeat (these may be signs of heart problems); severe allergic reaction signs such as hives, swelling of your face or throat, dizziness, or trouble breathing during or after your injection; signs of lung problems such as a new or worsening cough or difficulty breathing; unusual swelling in your legs or ankles; fever, chills, or signs of infection; severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea; confusion or changes in thinking; or if you are pregnant or think you might be pregnant.
when_it_works: This medicine begins working as soon as it is given, but you may not feel or notice the effects right away. Cancer treatment results are often seen over weeks to months. Your doctor will regularly check how well the medicine is working using physical exams, blood tests, and imaging scans. It is important to keep all follow-up appointments so your doctor can monitor your progress and adjust your treatment if needed.
special_populations: Pregnancy: This medicine can cause serious harm or death to an unborn baby. Do not use this medicine if you are pregnant. Use reliable birth control during treatment and for 7 months after your last dose. Tell your doctor immediately if you become pregnant. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed during treatment or for 7 months after your last dose, as the medicine may pass into breast milk and harm your baby. Elderly patients: Older adults may be at higher risk for certain side effects, especially heart problems. Your doctor will monitor you closely. Patients with heart disease: This medicine can weaken the heart. Tell your doctor if you have any history of heart problems before starting treatment. Your heart function will be tested before and during treatment.
